COARSE GRAINS
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO MARKETING IN COMING CROP YEAR

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: COARSE GRAINS
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO MARKETING IN COMING CROP YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement regarding the marketing of coarse grains.
Because of recent representations that have been made to the government, and in order to clarify the position for our farmers, I should like to make a brief statement in connection with the marketing of coarse grains for the coming crop year.
Hon. members will remember that this subject was fully discussed in this house last spring in connection with the passage of Bill 135. In introducing that bill I said in part:
The fourth amendment proposes to empower the governor in council by regulation to extend to oats and barley the regulations now applicable to wheat. Strong representations favouring the marketing of oats and barley through the wheat board have been received from farm organizations in both western and eastern Canada, among them the Canadian Council of Agriculture.
At present this is called the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
The government desires to meet the wishes of farm organizations in this regard, provided that a workable plan can be agreed upon. However, the government is well aware that the compulsory marketing of oats and barley through the board represents serious difficulties. The success of such an enterprise must be dependent on a large measure of agreement on policy matters as between organized farmers of both the producer and the consumer class, as well as on the co-operation of provincial governments. Therefore this government will wish to have concrete evidence of such agreement and such co-operation before it can assume the responsibility for putting this amendment into effect.
Again quoting from my same statement, I gave assurance that-
The government is prepared to take whatever steps lie within its power to assist in establishing marketing arrangements that will help to maintain economic and stable prices for Canadian agricultural products. The government must, however, be satisfied that any given scheme for this purpose is a practical one, a constitutional one, a workable one and one that will command the support of the interested groups concerned. Until it is satisfied that these conditions have been met. the govern-

ment will not be prepared to undertake the marketing of oats and barley through the wheat board. It will be noted in the resolution that marketing arrangements shall come into force only at the beginning of a crop year. I believe the attitude of the government in this regard will be understood by all hon. members who are familiar with grain marketing and related agricultural problems.
The position now is that one of the prairie provinces has introduced complementary legislation but the other two have not. However at a meeting of the western agricultural conference-namely, the provincial units of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in the four western provinces-in Saskatoon on January 20 to 22 inclusive, the following resolution was passed:
Be it resolved that a joint effort be made to enable the Canadian wheat board to be the sole marketing agency of coarse grains, and that any legislation giving the Canadian wheat board the same exclusive powers over the marketing of other grains as it now exercises over wheat, shall be based on the principle that the Canadian wheat board shall be an agency operating for the benefit and in the interest of grain producers, with a duty to sell grain for the best available price whether in export or domestic markets, and shall not be used as an instrument of government to control domestic policy; but full recognition of the importance of the livestock industry shall be given by the government of Canada, and that the government shall take adequate measures to establish necessary reserves of feed grains whenever such action is deemed necessary.
At the annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in the same city on January 24 to 28, the same resolution was presented and carried.
On February 21 of this year I met with a committee representing the western farm organizations and the Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba governments, who asked, first, for assurances that the implementation of Bill 135, when proclaimed, would meet the letter and the spirit of the resolution quoted above, and second, whether the federal government still considers it necessary that the three provincial legislatures must pass complementary legislation.
The resolution forwarded by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, which has been carefully reviewed, is not acceptable to the government. In the first place, if this resolution is intended to suggest that the Canadian wheat board as now constituted does not function in the best interests of the Canadian producers, this is a suggestion which I strenuously deny. Further, this resolution by its terms is contradictory, in that it would, on the one hand, require the board to sell "for the best available price whether in export or domestic markets" and at the same time to give "full recognition of the importance of the livestock industry."
In discussing the marketing of crops that are largely consumed within Canada, it is
Coarse Grains
obvious that the government of Canada cannot give any undertaking that it will become responsible for marketing coarse grains solely in the interests of the producer, and without regard to the interests of the consumer of those products. If the coarse grain producers of western Canada are not satisfied that the wheat board, as now constituted, is a satisfactory marketing agency for their coarse grains, then an obvious alternative is for the producers of coarse grains in western Canada to establish their own marketing agency. My colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, has on the order paper legislation designed to complement the marketing legislation of the provincial governments. Under such legislation, the producers can themselves establish a board to sell "for the best available price, whether in export or domestic markets." This assumes that to obtain "the best available price, whether in export or domestic markets," is in fact always in the best interest of the producers, which in my opinion is questionable, to say the least.
If, on the other hand, the western producers wish to market their oats and barley through the Canadian wheat board, and provided that their provincial governments will enact the necessary legislation, this government's position has not changed since I introduced Bill 135 in response to specific requests then made by the farm organizations.

maintopic: STRAIT OF CANSO
STRAIT OF CANSO
STRAIT OF CANSO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a statement to make which I hope will meet with the approval of the house. The board of engineers appointed jointly by the dominion government and the province of Nova Scotia last year to investigate the transportation facilities and their betterment at the strait of Canso have now submitted their report. The board, having given consideration to several methods of transportation across the strait, have reported in favour of the construction of a low-level bridge capable of handling both railway and vehicular traffic. The cost of constructing such a bridge is estimated at $13,500,000.
The board of engineers, consisting of D. S. Ellis, dean of the faculty of applied science of Queen's university, chairman, Arthur Surveyer, consulting engineer, of Montreal, and P. L. Pratley, consulting engineer, of Montreal, reported unfavourably on proposals for constructing a causeway, a tunnel or a high-level bridge. The board further reported that the present ferry system was operating at a loss and its discontinuance would result in a substantial saving which would more than pay for the probable* cost of maintaining and operating the proposed bridge.

It is evident that purchasing new ferry boats and rebuilding the ferry terminals would not materially improve the efficiency of the ferry services and would not give the uninterrupted passage which the public desires. The low-level bridge will, at all times, save fifty minutes in freight and passenger train schedule to the Sydneys.
The board of engineers had been called upon to review and report on the proposals to (a) construct a bridge capable of accommodating a single track railway and highway traffic, and which will permit the passage of vessels through the strait; (b) construct a causeway for railway and highway traffic which will permit the passage of vessels; (c) construct a tunnel for railway and highway traffic; or (d) provide improved railway ferry service across the strait. Of these projects, the board of engineers reported that the low-level short-span bridge was the only one which shows a saving on present operating costs and consequently was the only one which in their opinion was economically sound.
The board of engineers recommends that the bridge should be located between Cape Porcupine, on the mainland, and Balache Point, on Cape Breton island, where the strait is at its narrowest. The width at this point is slightly more than 3,000 feet. The proposal would require a bridge with a clearance of fourteen feet above water at high tide and a vertical lift span close to the Cape Breton shore to provide clearance of 156 feet for the passage of ships.
The government has decided to accept the recommendation of the board of engineers^-

I am also pleased to announce that the premier of Nova Scotia, after consultation with his colleagues, has agreed to contribute a portion of the cost of this project, details of which will be worked out later.
I believe the decision of the government to implement the recommendations of the board of engineers will not only provide an entirely satisfactory crossing of the strait, with consequent improvement in transportation generally in that part of Nova Scotia,

but with the entry of Newfoundland into confederation will also be of great importance in assisting the flow of traffic to and from the new province.
The board of engineers recommends that test borings, extending at least ten feet into the rock, should be made at the site of each of the proposed piers. The board further recommends that this boring program should be undertaken as early as possible-

-after the ice is gone from the strait so that construction plans can be started without delay. I am glad to notice .that my hon. friend is not interrupting me today.
It is estimated that the construction of the proposed low-level bridge would take about three years to complete, which is about the limit of the useful life of one of the railway car ferries now in operation between Mul-grave and Point Tupper.
The government will establish an authority or agency to carry out the recommendation of the board of engineers.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR EVENING SITTINGS 7.30 TO 10.30 UNTIL LAST SITTING DAY IN APRIL

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, March 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. St. Laurent:
That, except on Wednesdays, Mr. Speaker shall leave the chair at six o'clock p.m. until seven-thirty, and shall adjourn the house at ten-thirty p.m. without question put, unless the closure rule (standing order No. 39) be then in operation, this order to be in effect until and upon the last sitting day of the month of April.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROVISION FOR EVENING SITTINGS 7.30 TO 10.30 UNTIL LAST SITTING DAY IN APRIL
speechtext:
I ask that consideration be resumed of the motion that was made on March 7 as to the hours of sitting of the house. Hon. members will recall that there was a motion in effect which provided that until the completion of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne the house should resume its evening sitting at seven-thirty and adjourn at ten-thirty. The debate on the address has now been completed, and, unless consideration is given to this motion, the house will automatically go back to the standing order under which the house shall sit in the evening from eight o'clock until eleven o'clock.
As I stated when I put the motion before the house, I did so in order to give the house an opportunity to express its views upon the question, and not because I was recommending that the order then in effect should be continued. Since that time my attention has been called to the fact that, when the days are longer and finer, many hon. members like to take a stroll after dinner before coming back into the house. This motion, however, would merely extend to the end of April the changed evening hours of sitting. Perhaps it is optimistic to feel that prior to the end of April there will be very much opportunity for those agreeable strolls before coming into the house for the evening session. In any event, without asking the house to make one decision or the other, I submit this proposal so that the views of hon. members may be expressed and the desires of the greatest number followed.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PROVISION FOR EVENING SITTINGS 7.30 TO 10.30 UNTIL LAST SITTING DAY IN APRIL
speechtext:
I said when the motion was previously before the house that I felt this was not an effective way to deal with the problem, which many members have been considering for some time. I indicated that it was my intention to move an amendment which would result in the hours being from two to six and from eight to ten. In making such a motion now by way of amendment, I should like to point out that, as the Prime Minister

House of Commons
has said about the main motion, it is simply a suggestion put forward for consideration.
While I am a comparative newcomer in the house, one does not need to be here very long to recognize that the effectiveness of debate is related to a certain extent to the way in which the hours of the house accommodate themselves not only to the personal convenience of the members but also to the necessity for their doing a great deal of work outside the chamber. I think it is also to be considered that it must be a matter of great disadvantage to the press that the evening hour of adjournment is so late, because when the house sits until eleven o'clock it is some time after that before the press can deal with matters that have been discussed in the house.
My own feeling is that the members will do better work in the evening if the hours are from eight to ten, and afterwards they will be able to complete any necessary outside work without undue encroachment upon other arrangements they may make, and particularly upon their domestic arrangements where that may be a consideration. Moreover, by having a recess from six to eight an opportunity will be provided to meet people who wish to discuss various matters with the members, and members will be able to have their dinner and be back in the chamber at the time the house resumes.
The amendment I propose to move calls for the meeting of the house at two o'clock. The Prime Minister has indicated that in his opinion this presents some inconvenience to the cabinet. But I suggest that there is ample opportunity to adjust the hours of meeting of cabinet council, and that the business of government can be conducted more satisfactorily if the sitting hours that are arranged accommodate the members as well as the government itself-recognizing, of course, the importance of the task of the members of the cabinet and the responsibility that they assume. It seems to me that the government can well adjust the time of the regular meetings of cabinet council to meet this requirement, because, and properly so, the ministers during the course of certain debates find it convenient to carry on some of their other work in their own offices.
Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), that the resolution be amended as follows:
1.	That the following words be inserted after the word "that" in the first line of the resolution: "notwithstanding standing order No. 2, on and after Tuesday, March 15, 1949, the house shall meet at two o'clock in the afternoon of each sitting day, and that on and after this day" . . .
2.	That the words "eight o'clock" be substituted for the words "seven-thirty" in the third line of the

resolution; and that the words "ten o'clock p.m." be substituted for the words "ten-thirty p.m." in the fourth line of the resolution.
The effect would be that the resolution would read as follows:
That notwithstanding standing order No. 2, on and after Tuesday, March 15, 1949, the house shall meet at two o'clock in the afternoon of each sitting day, and that on and after this day, except on Wednesdays, Mr. Speaker shall leave the chair at six o'clock until eight o'clock p.m. and shall adjourn the house at ten p.m. without question put, unless the closure rule (standing order No. 39) be then in operation, this order to be in effect until and upon the last sitting day of the month of April.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR EVENING SITTINGS 7.30 TO 10.30 UNTIL LAST SITTING DAY IN APRIL
speechtext: If I may ask the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) a question-I do not want to infringe upon provincial rights at all in this-do I understand that his amendment includes Wednesday nights?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR EVENING SITTINGS 7.30 TO 10.30 UNTIL LAST SITTING DAY IN APRIL
speechtext: That would include Wednesday, and would mean an added hour each week in which to complete the business, as my hon. friend so earnestly desires.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR EVENING SITTINGS 7.30 TO 10.30 UNTIL LAST SITTING DAY IN APRIL
speechtext: No.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR EVENING SITTINGS 7.30 TO 10.30 UNTIL LAST SITTING DAY IN APRIL
speechtext: I was thinking so much of the insistence of the hon. member that we sit Wednesday night that I made a mistake. The resolution would have the effect of adding one hour a week through the longer sitting on Wednesday afternoon, but we would not sit Wednesday evening.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR EVENING SITTINGS 7.30 TO 10.30 UNTIL LAST SITTING DAY IN APRIL
speechtext: Then I am sorry; I cannot support you.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR EVENING SITTINGS 7.30 TO 10.30 UNTIL LAST SITTING DAY IN APRIL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have been here long enough to appreciate the fact that it is extremely difficult to find sitting hours that will accommodate all hon. members and enable them, as well as the members of the cabinet, to do the work that must be done. I would be quite willing to go along with the old hours of three to six and eight to eleven, though I do appreciate getting home half an hour earlier. The point I want to make is that there is a definite objection to the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition. Today we have set up the standing committees, which usually sit in the morning from eleven to one. By the time you get to your office and put away your papers it is at least 1.15, and that leaves only three-quarters of an hour in which to get lunch and be back in the house. That would be an impossible situation; and while I am not particularly in favour of the original motion, I am definitely against the amendment for the reason I have stated.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR EVENING SITTINGS 7.30 TO 10.30 UNTIL LAST SITTING DAY IN APRIL
speechtext:
I want to say a few words about starting an hour earlier. I believe the hon. member who has

just spoken (Mr. Maclnnis) pointed to a serious situation which would develop. It is true that the committees generally start work at eleven o'clock; and it may surprise the leader of the opposition to learn that many times, because there is a large number of permanent and special committees of this house, it is difficult to secure a quorum in order to get the work of a committee started. Sometimes we have to close our eyes and ignore the fact that we lack a quorum.
In spite of what hon. members opposite may say, I think it would be impossible to have the committees begin work at ten o'clock, no matter how hard we might try to do it. The question of changing the hours of sitting should be studied thoroughly; but we should be careful to see that the work of the permanent and special committees of the house is not interfered with, because that would defeat the very end we are trying to achieve-that of accelerating at least to some extent the work of this house.
In all sincerity I say it is impossible to have the committees start before eleven o'clock in the morning, and I have had a good deal of experience in that regard. It is also impossible to adjourn much before one o'clock. If the amendment were adopted, only one hour would be left before the opening of the house, and I submit that under such conditions we could not do our work properly. I am sure the leader of the opposition agrees that committees must function freely in this or any other legislature, and if we curtail their work to any extent, instead of expediting the work of this house we shall be retarding it. So far as I am concerned, after many years of experience with the committees of this house, I must vote against the amendment.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR EVENING SITTINGS 7.30 TO 10.30 UNTIL LAST SITTING DAY IN APRIL
speechtext:
The hon.
member who has just spoken has had a great deal of experience in committee work, but I find myself in disagreement with the view he has put forward. It seems to me it would meet the convenience of hon. members if our committees were called at an earlier hour, and perhaps the result would be better all round if we closed at ten o'clock and took the extra hour off at night. I think that would overcome the objection of the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette).

maintopic: PROVISION FOR EVENING SITTINGS 7.30 TO 10.30 UNTIL LAST SITTING DAY IN APRIL
speechtext:
In some respects I agree with the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank); one of our points of agreement is that neither of us is a tete-a-tete man. I agree wholeheartedly that the work of our committees is an important phase of the work of this house, but for the life of me I cannot see why the hours of meeting
House of Commons
of the committees cannot be adjusted. A great many of us are here at eight-thirty in the morning, have our breakfast and are looking after our correspondence by nine o'clock. On the average that work is cleared up by ten o'clock, when we could attend committee meetings, and those committees could rise at noon.
There is another thought I should like to put forward. As part of our democratic parliamentary set-up we depend a great deal upon the press, and I know that many members of the press do not leave this house until after midnight, sometimes not until one or two o'clock in the morning. Surely we could give a little consideration to the gentlemen of the press without interfering at all with the splendid work done by the committees of the house. I have not been here as long as some hon. members, but this is my tenth session, and at times I have belonged to three or four standing committees, some of which have been meeting simultaneously.
I believe that with a little thought and adjustment we could arrange to have those committees sit from ten to twelve, in order that the house might meet at more convenient hours, thus benefiting all hon. members.
I would hope that we might seriously consider, on a non-party basis, the possibility of changing to the hours proposed, two to six and eight to ten, which I am sure would prove to be in the interests of the committees as well as of this house itself.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR EVENING SITTINGS 7.30 TO 10.30 UNTIL LAST SITTING DAY IN APRIL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I suggest that the question be put? I for one would like to enter into the argument, but surely this is largely a matter of personal desire and opinion. We can neither dissuade nor persuade each other; therefore I suggest that we take the vote.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR EVENING SITTINGS 7.30 TO 10.30 UNTIL LAST SITTING DAY IN APRIL
speechtext:
Before the vote is taken I would like to hear the views of hon. members on the possibility of sitting through from two o'clock until eight o'clock, without any dinner adjournment, or from three to nine, whichever may meet with their approval. In discussing this matter I have heard hon. members say you could not get a sufficient number in the house at that time to carry on. Come in here any night at eight o'clock, half an hour after the house opens, and you will not find more than forty or fifty members in their seats; the other two hundred could be having their dinner at that time. I believe many hon. members feel as I do and would like to get out in the evening for a swim or to play golf or to do various things, and I am sure this change would suit many who do not wish to sit here night after night. For my part, I would just as soon sit

House of Commons
in the House of Commons from ten to eleven, as I would sit down at the Lord Elgin hotel.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR EVENING SITTINGS 7.30 TO 10.30 UNTIL LAST SITTING DAY IN APRIL
speechtext: Speaking personally, and perhaps from a selfish point of view, I think the silliest thing this House of Commons ever did was to attempt to save this half hour and ruin everybody's dinner. I live about a mile and a half from the parliament buildings. I like to walk home once a day, and I like to be able to say hello to my wife without doing it on the run. I intend to walk home before dinner, and I intend to do what I usually do before dinner, irrespective of what rules are made. I am going to take the two hours, and I think that is what all members should do.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR EVENING SITTINGS 7.30 TO 10.30 UNTIL LAST SITTING DAY IN APRIL
speechtext:
The
member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) has laid great stress on the work of the committees. My experience has been that the committees usually meet on Tuesdays and Thursdays.^ I think we should adjust the hours of sittings of the house, which meets daily, and adjust the committee hours later -even ten-thirty to twelve-thirty; we could get our two hours in just the same. I make this observation, sir, in the hope that members will keep it in mind when making their decision.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROVISION FOR EVENING SITTINGS 7.30 TO 10.30 UNTIL LAST SITTING DAY IN APRIL
speechtext:
I think we have had an effective demonstration of the difficulty of fixing hours that will suit the convenience of everyone. I should be reluctant to have the convenience of the members of the government, or even of the members of the house, put into competition with the convenience of the members of the press gallery. Nevertheless, it is evident no solution can be found that will suit everyone. As the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has said, this is not a matter of government policy. If the house sits from two until six, it involves inconvenience for the members of the government. If the house sits at other hours, it involves inconvenience for other members of the house and, as we have been told, for the gentlemen of the press. I think the only possible remedy is for each of us to record his vote on the amendment and on the motion in accordance with what most closely approximates his own convenience.
Amendment (Mr. Drew) negatived.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN NAVY
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence in connection with a reported statement by Vice-Admiral Grant at a meeting in Toronto of the Toronto branch of the Naval Officers' Association last Friday evening when he stated that Russia had four times the number of U-boats that Hitler had. I asked a similar question last week in the form of a notice of question. The minister said that Canada's navy had no submarines. Perhaps the minister does not know, but I should like to find out.

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN NAVY
speechtext:
The hon. member asked on Friday about the policy of the government with regard to submarines. I take it from what I could hear of what he has just said that his question today relates to the same subject. The submarine is still generally regarded not as a defensive weapon but as an offensive weapon, used to destroy naval vessels and shipping of an enemy. Canada has no aggressive intentions. The only possible aggressor at the present time has not a large surface fleet.
It is the view of the government and its advisers that it would be a waste of Canada's resources to go in for the very expensive business of having submarines. When we need a submarine for anti-submarine training we have been able to make arrangements with the Royal Navy or the United States navy or to engage in joint exercises such as those now going on in the Caribbean. We believe that this represents the sensible approach to the problem of co-operation in defence. Co-operation is the only way in which Canada or any other country can defend itself today, and is also the only way in which peace can be secured. Obviously Canada could not and should not duplicate the defensive activities of every great power. Our object is to do what we should for our own immediate defence against direct attack and to work with other friendly nations in joint defence so as to preserve the peace.

My hon. friend will remember the amendments that were made last year to include the logging industry in the unemployment insurance scheme. The latter figure of $3,120 is now the maximum amount which salaried workers can earn and still be covered by unemployment insurance. In addition to a higher percentage of unplaced applicants being covered by unemployment insurance, there are actually fewer persons out of work today who are not covered by this form of assistance than at the same date in any earlier post-war year. At the beginning of March, 1948, for example, there were close to 5,000 persons registered for work in Vancouver who were not active claimants for unemployment insurance, whereas today there are only 3,000. The comparative figures for 1947 and 1946 were 7,500 and 8,200 respectively.

This is an indication that the situation is righting itself. The total amount paid out during February in the form of unemployment insurance benefits in Vancouver was $830,000. One-fifth of this amount was paid by the federal government. In addition to this assistance a number of agencies have formed a local community council in Vancouver which is providing aid to persons temporarily unemployed. During the month of January, some 8,000 meals and 2,000 beds were provided by these local groups. A number of borderline cases also received assistance from the city and province during January. This assistance from these various local sources totaled about $7,000.
Of the 25,000 unplaced applicants registered with the national employment service in Vancouver at the beginning of March about 3,000 were veterans. This number is
2,000	less than at the same date last year. It might be added that, based on interviews

Labour Conditions
made recently with nearly 500 unemployed veterans over forty-five years of age in Vancouver, it was found that one-third had a fairly adequate income for current purposes from pensions, from superannuation, or from other sources.
There are a number of special factors which might be mentioned bearing on the present situation in Vancouver. It is estimated that some 80,000 workers have been added to the labour force in British Columbia since 1946, bringing it up to a total of 425,000 at present. This represents an increase of 23 per cent, whereas in Canada as a whole the corresponding growth in the labour force has been only 10 per cent. The expansion of the labour force in Vancouver has been at least as great as that for the whole province.
The labour force in British Columbia and in Vancouver has a relatively high proportion of workers over forty-five years of age. Thirty-five per cent of all workers in British Columbia are in this category. In Canada as a whole the corresponding percentage is 31. In British Columbia, where much of the work is of a strenuous character, older workers ordinarily constitute a more difficult placement problem.
Each winter there is a considerable influx of workers into Vancouver, not only from sections of British Columbia, but also from outside the province. A large part of this movement is of a temporary nature. Most of these workers are regularly employed in other occupations for most of the year. They come to Vancouver only during the period when employment is slack, as is the case, for instance, with many farm workers from the prairie provinces and from the interior of British Columbia. Of the 25,000 unplaced applicants at the beginning of March, it is estimated that close to 6,000 moved to Vancouver within the past six months. About one-third of these persons are from other parts of British Columbia while the remaining two-thirds are from outside the province.
A large number of the logging camps in British Columbia close down temporarily at the end of December each year. Many of the released woods workers move into Vancouver at this time. This year these camps were not able to reopen as quickly as they ordinarily do because of heavy snow and unusually cold weather. Most of the mills are now open and a steady stream of men is going back to work.
The cold weather in January reduced building operations to a minimum. A large building program is again getting under way in Vancouver, and with the milder weather employment is opening up rapidly. Already during 1949 construction contracts awarded

total more in value than during the same period last year. This follows the same upward trend in construction that was in evidence throughout 1948, as the following figures for Vancouver indicate:

The lack of rain, and the cold weather throughout the coastal area during January, resulted in hydroelectric power shortages which caused a 30 per cent cut in industrial power. As a result of rains during February the power situation is now back to normal, and those workers temporarily laid off have returned to their jobs.
It would appear from this report that the unemployment situation in Vancouver was a temporary one. The peak of unemployment was reached in February in Vancouver as it was throughout the country as a whole. Since then the number of workers applying at the national employment service in Vancouver who remain unplaced has been falling off with increasing rapidity. Local officers report that more jobs are opening up every day as construction, logging and other seasonal industries get into full swing.
With incomes and investment expected to remain at high levels during 1949, the employment outlook during the coming months is quite favourable in British Columbia, as it is in other parts of Canada.
No one in this House of Commons, I feel sure, needs to be told that the variations in employment each year in Canada are greatly dependent on the seasons. This is no new thing. It has been a condition which has always existed and, in my opinion, will always prevail. The situation in British Columbia has been, to a very large extent, a seasonal one and the shock of the effect on the individual lives of our workers has been, in very large measure, cushioned by unemployment insurance. The parliament of Canada has reason to congratulate itself upon this very fine legislation. As I indicated a moment ago, in February alone in Vancouver $830,000 was paid in unemployment insurance benefits.
In conclusion I should like to say that there-has been some criticism of the delay in the payment of some of the claims. I do not wish to go into details, as most hon. members know the mechanics of the act, but I am assured by the commission that the situation is practically cleared up, and we hope to have things moving expeditiously from now on.

speechtext:
On March 3, as
reported at page 1093 of Hansard, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) referred to a provision in section 9 of the act setting up the Department of Reconstruction and Supply, which provision he asserted would require the tabling of an annual report of the department.
Section 7, to which the hon. member referred, is in the Department of Reconstruction Act, 1944, not in the Department of Reconstruction and Supply Act, 1945. The Department of Reconstruction and Supply was formed by the merger of two departments, munitions and supply and reconstruction, and the former department was not required by statute to table a report. Therefore I state again that the tabling of an annual report on the general departmental activities of the Department of Reconstruction and Supply is not mandatory, since a report, if any, would be required only in respect of those functions originally within the purview of the Department of Reconstruction. Consequently no consolidated report for the department was prepared in the past, and the branches or agencies constituting the department either placed reports before parliament or were reported upon orally by the minister.
These branches and agencies, which I believe numbered ten in 1945, subsequently have been either abolished or transferred to other departments. There now remain only three branches or agencies identified with the Department of Reconstruction and Supply. They are Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, whose annual report will be tabled shortly; the Canadian travel bureau, whose report also will be tabled shortly; and finally the public projects branch, for which a report could be prepared and submitted to parliament if it is felt that the oral reports already given by my predecessor concerning the public projects branch, and the relevant questions which have been answered in this house during this session of parliament, need

Inquiries of the Ministry to be supplemented by such a document. Personally I do not believe it would add anything to what is already on record.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, February 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Garson that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The last time this measure was before the house, on February 18, the member for Peace River (Mr. Low) put on the record our attitude towards this motion. In view of the fact many days have passed since that time, I should like to refresh the memory of the members of the House of Commons by quoting very briefly some of the things he said. I refer to page 675 of Hansard.
X sincerely hope that the contents of this resolution for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council does not constitute the whole of the program the government intends to bring in at this session in connection with the very serious matter of prices and distribution facing the country today.
Further on, he said:
The rank and file of the Canadian people are not asking for more control; but they are asking for relief from the burden of high living costs. People generally are waking up to the fact that the government itself is perhaps the chief culprit in this whole matter of extremely high prices.
The member for Peace River then went on to show how high taxation has raised the price of goods to the people.
In concluding, he had this to say:
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say that the people of this country are going to be bitterly disappointed if the government fails to supplement these orders, which are now in the form of resolutions, by positive action aimed at reducing the cost of living. I declare there is no better place to start than in their own taxation structure, especially the iniquitous sales tax.
At a later stage, he said:
-and using the modest subsidies which we have proposed from time to time on selected items used

Transitional Measures Act from day to day by families, which subsidies could be paid for not out of taxation but with interest-free money-
I intend to expand upon some of these points, but before doing so I want to refer briefly to some of the criticisms, made by members of the C.C.F. party, of the statement made by the member for Peace River concerning his trip to England. The member for Peace River referred to the fact that, while he was over in Great Britain, he found a great deal of discontent in regard to some of the controls. He referred to those controls, showing the results that they had had upon the economy of that country. Frankly, I must admit I was amazed at some of the extreme language used by members of the C.C.F. in criticizing that statement. One member even went so far as to describe it is a despicable attack upon Great Britain.
I should like to point out that at no time did the member for Peace River attack either the people of Britain or Great Britain herself. His criticism was leveled against certain controls and the results those controls had had upon the British economy. It seems to me that the main trouble with the C.C.F. is that they regard their type of government as the embodiment of the aims and objects of the people. Hence, they insist that an attack upon that government is an attack upon the people, which of course is another matter entirely. I would say that it is a very dangerous attitude of mind. It is the type of psychology found in men like Hitler, Mussolini and Stalin, and it breeds intolerance.
Let me ask the C.C.F. this question. When they attack the policies of the Liberal government, as I have heard them do time and again, sometimes viciously, would they agree that when they are attacking the policies of the Liberal party they are attacking the Canadian people or Canada? I am satisfied they would say, nonsense. Then, I would say that in accusing the leader of this group, when he spoke about certain controls in England, of having made an attack against the British people, that was also nonsense.
I should like to refer specifically to some of the statements made by the member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Knight) which are found on page 692 of Hansard. The member for Saskatoon City suggested that, perhaps, the member for Peace River was not familiar with conditions overseas because he had only made one trip to Great Britain. I hope he will appreciate the fact that I have known England fairly well in the past. I believe I was born in the same year as the member for Saskatoon City and I also happened to come to Canada in the same year as he did. I have been back on many occasions. I spent four years overseas in the first war. I have many

relatives over there, and I carry on correspondence with them fairly frequently. I say that, judging by the correspondence I have had from my relatives over there, I find that their criticism of many of the policies carried on in Britain today is just as severe as the criticism which was made by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). May I say that my relatives cannot be considered to be wealthy people; they are just the ordinary middle class, and probably the controls which are exercised in Britain today fall more heavily upon the middle class than upon any other class.
But let me call another witness on this question. I should like to refer to the fact that one of the senior members of the Labour party in Britain has been most critical of some of the control policies carried out by that party. I should like to quote from a speech made by the hon. member for Nottingham South, H. Norman Smith, on Wednesday, December 12, 1945. I shall quote from the official record. He had this to say:
I have been in this Labour party nearly thirty-nine years.
Evidently he was one of the senior members of the party in so far as length of membership is concerned. He continued:
There are very few hon. or right hon. gentlemen on this side of the house who have the length of membership of this party that I have.
Therefore he was speaking with some authority. He continued:
I want, in my turn, to use arguments calculated to bring my hon. friends on this side of the house into the division lobby against these proposals-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Shame.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
because I am absolutely certain that, as the hon. member for East Aberdeen has already stated, these proposals open the way to the influences which broke the second Labour government in 1931. If the house gives effect to these proposals, only a miracle will save the third Labour government from the fate that overtook the second.
By the way, the title of this speech is "Parliament abdicates financial control". Then he went on to mention the fact that in many instances the policies of the Labour government are very similar to the policies of the Liberal party. I noticed that when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) spoke he pointed out to members of the C.C.F. that many of the measures in operation today were measures which were first of all started by the Liberal party. Then Mr. Smith had this to say:
It is a matter no doubt for congratulation to the tiny remnant of Liberals, most of whose party have been swept out of this house, that, though their party is now shattered and almost nonexistent, their ideals are triumphing on the front bench of the Labour party.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. member a question? Would he say that the barter

agreements which Great Britain is entering into are economic Liberalism?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I would say that the international financial policies of Britain since the war have been, to a very large extent, dominated by the Bretton Woods agreement, under which she agreed to make the pound convertible into dollars, and as a consequence she lost, or had to reduce, her exports by about $800 million. So far as the barter agreements are concerned, she is being forced into them by economic necessity, but she may not be able to carry them on unless changes are made in the Bretton Woods agreement.	[DOT]
I should like to quote another statement from Mr. Smith. He said:
Never, in the whole of history, was it proposed to give such tremendous power to an authority as is contemplated in the Bretton Woods scheme. Neither Hitler nor Mussolini, at their respective zeniths, not even the Roman emperors in Rome's palmiest days, had such tremendous power as it is proposed to confer upon this fund.
And in order to emphasize the need for maintaining financial controls in the hands of the government of Britain, instead of the hands of international financiers, he had this to say:
The Labour and socialist movement in this country completely failed then to understand that, if there is a class war, it is not between employers on one side and workers on the other, because neither employers nor workers have the real power when it comes to an economic showdown. The real class war is between, on the one hand, the few people who control finance and, on the other hand, the rest of the community, in which category I would include anybody who works for a living.
I quoted this statement to show that fortunately there are members in the Labour party who appreciate the dangers of the control policies of the Labour party today, or at least the extent to which they have relinquished certain financial controls and turned them over to the hands of an international authority.
Apparently the hon. member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Knight) did not like the remarks of the hon. member for Peace River. He suggested that the hon. member for Peace River might have got his information from the wrong sources. He implied that it might possibly have been from Oswald Mosley. I will read what he said, as reported at page 692 of Hansard:
X am not going to suggest that one of the people he saw was Oswald Mosley-but from the opinions he expressed, I should think such opinions might easily have been garnered from that source.
I do not know whether that statement was supposed to be witty or whether it was supposed to have anything behind it; but let me point out-and before I make this statement
29087-91J
Transitional Measures Act let me say quite clearly that I am not suggesting for one minute that the C.C.F. as the national socialist party of Canada is the counterpart of the national socialist party of Germany; but in view of the fact that the hon. member thought it worth while to try to link us up with Oswald Mosley, I should like to say that there is a far greater affinity between the ideas of the C.C.F. as the national socialist party of Canada and the national socialist party of Germany than there is with the Social Credit party. I say that for this reason. Both of these parties believe in centralization. We believe in the greatest possible degree of decentralization. Both of these parties believe in the multiplicity of controls, and we believe that controls should be used only to the extent absolutely necessary to maintain the efficient operation of the economy. Both of these parties believe in a very large degree of public investment. We believe that public investment should be the residual action necessary to maintain the optimum development of the resources of the country. Therefore I say that the hon. member for Saskatoon City would have been far more logical if he had addressed his remarks relating to Oswald Mosley to members of his own party instead of to members of this party.
Then the hon. member wondered whether the hon. member for Peace River had seen the results of public investment in England. Mind you, the hon. member for Peace River had not criticized any of the public investments which had been made in that country; but the hon. member for Saskatoon City suggests that he might have seen the fine houses which have been built, the power development schemes and other investments. The point I want to make is this: just because fine public projects have been carried out in England under public investment, it does not mean that you have to agree with certain control policies that have been instituted in that country.
I was in England in 1938 at the time of Munich, and I spoke to a number of school teachers who had just come back from Germany. They recounted to me in glowing terms some of the public projects they had seen in Germany. They referred to the wonderful roads which had been built; they referred to the public buildings and the development of power. They referred to the reforms which had been carried out in agriculture; but on the other hand they were most bitter in their denunciations of the controls and the degree of regimentation which were being carried out in that country.
I am satisfied that if the hon. member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Knight) were permitted to go behind the iron curtain today he would see great development projects on the way,.

Transitional Measures Act projects developed by public investment- power developments, road-building programs, great cities being built in Siberia and across the Urals. But does that mean to say tor one moment that, because he appreciates what is being done under public investment, he must also at the same time agree with the type oi controls and regimentation carried out under the soviet regime today?
Then the hon. member proceeds to state that he deplores this attack upon Great Britain. I have already pointed out that at no time did the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) attack Great Britain. He attacked merely a certain control policy; and I resent bitterly the implication that members of this group are anti-British. Indeed, I think members of the C.C.F. could earn that description to a far greater degree than we could.
The hon. member goes on to say:
The state in which she found herself was that of bankruptcy-a bankruptcy which was caused by her war effort.
Unfortunately that is only half the story, because even if there had been no war she would have found herself in a difficult position today. As proof of that I would quote from the interim report of the European recovery program, sections 26, 27 and 28 of which state:
The long-term problem of western Europe is thus one of maintaining a high standard of living for a dense population, in a world where it is no longer the predominant source of manufactured supplies. Even in 1938, nearly one-half of the world's output of manufactures was produced outside western Europe; now the proportion is much higher. For many years, the problem of paying for these supplies had been growing. Between 1913 and 1939 imports from overseas were increasing but exports were declining; exports of manufactures of the main industrial nations fell by over one-quarter. The market for some of Europe's manufactures was becoming more and more restricted.
Even if there had been no world wars, this course of world economic development would sooner or later have forced a change in western Europe's economic structure. The loss of her predominance in manufacturing would have compelled an adaption in the nature of her exports, and specialization in those types of products where her competitive advantage was greatest. The gradual reduction, in more recently developed continents, of advantages of inexpensive land and labour would have forced Europe to reduce her dependence upon imports of primary products.
Then, referring to the years between the wars, it goes on to state:
But although the position of western Europe in the world, economy has been progressively weakened during this century and particularly after 1913, there have been props and stays which concealed the weakness of the structure. Until 1913 western Europe was a large exporter of capital; its exports and invisible earnings far exceeded its imports. When after 1918 exports failed to recover to the 1913 level, the margin available for investment abroad was reduced. Gradually during the interwar years, the annual rate of foreign investment

decreased further, until by 1938 there was no net investment at all. These trends could not have persisted indefinitely. Western Europe could only have continued to import more and export less by living on capital.
I say that demonstrates clearly that Great Britain's position today is not merely the result of either the second great war or the first one, but is the result of the expansion in industrialization in different parts of the world outside of Europe.
Then the hon. member saw fit to go on as follows:
Everyone knows that. And, if I may say so, that war effort was not exerted wholly on her own behalf. Let us not forget that for many days and months she stood alone.
I would suggest members of the C.C.F. party should be the very last to refer to that matter; because they, and they alone, were the party who in 1939 took the stand that Britain should continue to stand alone, that the C.C.F. were opposed to any military participation overseas. Farther down in his speech, the hon. member apparently thought he should try to become humorous. After referring to the difficulties in which Great Britain had found herself, he said:
And let me say that she did not try to meet her debts with funny money, either,
I always regret to hear members of the C.C.F. echoing the speeches made by reactionaries in this country-because there are many reactionaries in Canada who are trying to make the people believe that the use of national money would be a resort to funny money. The C.C.F. are playing into their hands every time they use that expression either in or out of the house. I am not saying all members of the C.C.F. do that; there are some who understand the need for national money, as much as we do.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Do they know what funny money is?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: All we have to do is to go back to the years after 1929 when the purchasing power of the dollar hit a new high in this country. In the nineteen-thirties the purchasing power of the dollar was so high that you could buy five bushels of wheat for a dollar, you could buy six pounds of butter for a dollar; twenty pounds of pork and twenty pounds of dressed turkey. I know whereof I speak because those are the prices I got in 1932 for those products. I am satisfied that farmers are not looking forward to the day when the purchasing power of the dollar is increased so that anything like that can happen again. I suppose the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would say that it is not necessary to put the value of the dollar that high; but how high are you going to put it?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If you ever get started you will not be able to stop it.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: As the hon. member for Peace River says, it is not an easy thing to stop once you have started. Once you start forcing prices down it is hard to put the brakes on. I know that in the past the C.C.F. have advocated rolling back prices to January 1, 1946, but that would mean lower prices for our primary producers. Would the government have been justified in keeping the prices of agricultural products down to the January 1, 1946, level? I say most definitely no, and for this reason. For many years the farmers of Canada had to produce at world market prices which were far below the cost of production, and as a result of that they were driven heavily into debt. The only way any concern that is driven into debt can get out of debt is to receive prices considerably above the cost of production. During the 1930's the farmers took world market prices far below the cost of production, and since 1942 they have been compelled to take prices less than world market prices. In all fairness to agriculture, owing to the fact that we compelled them to carry on under conditions that forced them into debt, they have a right now to expect us to allow conditions to exist that will make it possible to pay for that debt. When you say that the farmers should not be allowed an increase in prices above the 1945 level I say you are not being fair to agriculture.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Would the hon. member not say that the farmers were better off in 1945 than they are at the present time?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I would say that they are better off now, unquestionably, and I will tell you why. It is true that in 1945 the farmers could buy for less than they pay today, but do not forget this important point

-it should not be necessary tor me to remind the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) about this because he is a farmer. Farmers only spend a percentage of their income on goods but they get the increased prices on their total production. If they spend 50 per cent of their income on goods, then they are penalized to the extent that the prices of those goods have risen but they receive the increased prices on their total production. For instance, let us take the man who rents a farm. He has to pay one-third for rent and he only has two-thirds left. If you put prices down it is going to make it that much harder for him to pay his rent if he is paying it on a cash basis.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The trouble was, they took the ceilings off the things the farmer had to buy but kept them on what he had to sell.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is only partly true, but I think the hon. member for Melfort will agree that on the whole agriculture has not done too badly since 1945. The concern of agriculture today is not about the prices they are getting at the present time. The fear is as to what they are going to get in the future.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I agree with you there.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The farmers of this country would not demand for one minute that they be allowed the increased prices represented by world market prices today if in return they were guaranteed stabilized prices in the future, but up to date they have not received that guarantee. I notice that the hon. member for Melfort opposed the depreciation of the dollar. I presume the reason he did so was that the Conservative party happened to be advocating the depreciation of the dollar. I was the only member of the house who spoke against appreciating the dollar to parity with the United States dollar. After it had happened, some of the Conservatives objected, but I pointed out that as far as agriculture was concerned it was always opposed to having an appreciated dollar. The hon. member for Melfort criticized the idea of depreciating the dollar, and then went on to say, "look how the farmers suffered during the 1930's when we had a depreciated dollar." We did not have a depreciated dollar in the 1930's. He is so badly mixed up that he is criticizing the very thing he should not criticize. In the 1930's we had an appreciated dollar, and the reason that agriculture ran into the difficulties that it did was the fact that we had an appreciated dollar instead of a depreciated one. The hon. member for Melfort said that the pound would only fetch $3.86. What he should have said was that in those years you could buy a pound for only
Transitional Measures Act $3.86 instead of having to pay $4.85 for it. In other words, it had appreciated approximately 18 to 20 per cent with the result that, when we were paid in sterling in England for our wheat and the pound sterling was converted back to dollars, instead of the farmer receiving $4.85 he only got $3.86 for it. That is an appreciated dollar, which is the very thing that the hon. member was advocating.

One of the great difficulties that we ran into in the 1930's was the fact that our competitors, Australia, New Zealand and the Argentine, had their currencies depreciated below the pound sterling. We had our currency appreciated approximately 20 per cent above. Therefore those countries had an advantage of about 45 per cent in competing with us for the European market.

Well, it was fairly obvious. Now I am speaking without any question about the rules, and I will refer to the very few words I said previously. I indicated I believed . it was a point of order to which I had spoken, though that does not need to be debated. I can now deal with what I said at that time. I pointed out that this resolution calls for consideration of the continuance of certain emergency measures, and that before we proceed to consider those emergency measures and the wisdom of dealing with them, this house is entitled to an explanation of what the emergency is and what the reasons are that in 1949 we should be called upon to regard as still continuing an emergency which related to the war that ended in 1945.
On Friday last, when the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) pointed out what would be dealt with today, he stated that we would be dealing with a measure which would determine whether there would be a continuance of the controls over housing, and certain other matters. That is not what we are considering on this motion. What we are considering, and the only thing we are considering on this motion, is whether or not there is an emergency which justifies the continuance of wartime emergency powers or whether, if that emergency has passed, other procedures should be followed to deal with those things which the government or any hon. member wishes to bring before this house.
As I have stated already in this chamber, there can be no question but that the government must deal in some way with the housing situation, and must deal with it in a more effective way than in the past. But there is absolutely no necessity to carry forward wartime emergency powers in order that this house may deal effectively with any measure relating to the subject of housing which this house, under any circumstances, can have power to deal with. The time has come for the government to place before parliament a statute dealing with the housing problem, and to provide in that statute clear and unmistakable terms which can be understood by both landlords and tenants so the confusion which exists today may be brought to an end. Moreover the government itself has clearly demonstrated that it no longer believes there is an emergency in relation to this matter which would justify a continuance of the war emergency powers. It seems to me that in putting forward this resolution the government has overlooked the effect of the proposal it made to the provincial governments. This government said to the provincial governments that if they were prepared to request the federal authority to vacate the field of housing the dominion was prepared to aban-

don its emergency powers in respect of housing in such areas. If that is so, by that very act the government has said emphatically that it no longer regards this as the type of emergency which calls for action of necessity by the dominion government; and unless there is such an emergency which compels the dominion government to act, and in which it has no choice but to act, then there is no emergency which entitles it to circumvent the constitution.
Oh, I can almost hear the suggestion being made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) that I am back on the subject of the constitution and dominion-provincial rights. Well, I hope that by now the minister has read a very important judgment delivered in Manitoba last Thursday, because that judgment will have considerable bearing on this whole question since it demonstrates very clearly the kind of emergency that justifies the continuance of these powers and the relation of parliament itself to the extension of this arbitrary centralization of what otherwise would be provincial affairs.
By this motion parliament is asked to declare that the emergency arising out of the war still continues. Every hon. member who votes in support of this resolution declares by his vote that in his opinion the emergency arising out of the war still continues. That is a very important question of fact, which calls for the careful consideration and judgment of every hon. member. There is often a tendency to speak of lawyers in rather contemptuous terms; sometimes it is done jokingly, sometimes otherwise. But it must be remembered that there are occasions when lawyers in parliament are very useful and helpful to those who are called upon to be lawmakers, who are called upon to accept the responsibility of passing laws which will affect the lives and daily activities of our people across the whole of this country. A declaration by parliament that an emergency of this kind still exists is a declaration of fact which affects a very wide field of laws which in turn at some time must be interpreted by the courts. In voting on this resolution I submit that it is of the utmost importance for every member to consider carefully what will be the effect of his vote. The law is important. The making of laws within the jurisdiction of this parliament is the responsibility of the members of this parliament. Therefore it is important that each of us ask what the issue is on this resolution now before us.
As I suggested a few moments ago, the issue has been clearly decided by a unanimous judgment of the appeal court of Manitoba, delivered last Thursday. The style of cause is Nolan vs Hallet and Carey Limited. The five judges of that court were unanimous in
Transitional Measures Act their decision, and they have greatly assisted anyone who wishes to consider the law involved in this case. The judgment will merit consideration. Let us see what the issue is as defined by these jurists.
I quote now from the judgment rendered in this case by Mr. Justice Adamson.
It is going a long way to say or suggest that the federal parliament can invade the provincial field without any onus on it to justify such action. The justification must be some matter which has assumed paramount national importance, such as a national emergency of such proportions as to imperil the nation. To say that those who impugn such legislation must bring "clear evidence" of such emergency is to put a great national constitutional matter on the level of private dispute over a contract. A "national emergency," or a matter which has become of paramount importance to the dominion as a whole, which requires "clear evidence" of its existence, is inconceivable. An emergency of the kind required for the dominion to invade the provincial field must of its nature be self-evident, generally known and accepted, and be something of which the courts must take judicial notice. Anything less than this would be a mere pretext.
A little later the same judge said this:
Both the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945, and order in council 1292 recite and rely for their justification and legality upon the "continued existence" of the national emergency arising out of the war against Germany and Japan. Order in council 1292 is directed to a supposed economic emergency. The first question, therefore, is to inquire whether there was or was not an economic emergency-
The judgment then proceeds to discuss the type of emergency that should be looked for in this case.
Granting, for the sake of argument, that an economic emergency-except during an actual war-can ever justify an invasion of the provincial legislative field by the dominion: What are the facts and what is the evidence in this case?
In the record there is no evidence whatever of an economic emergency. What the emergency was, was not suggested.
This House of Commons is in precisely that position. What the emergency is upon which we are asked to say that we should proceed with this National Emergency Transitional Powers Act is not even suggested. I submit that the course followed by the government in this respect is an affront to parliament. We are simply told: Here is a resolution this all-wise government has presented; it is your job to vote for that resolution without a word being said in support of it.
Just let me read further from this judgment. There is mention of whether or not there is an emergency such as to justify these powers, and I quote:
' In 1947 (1) the national income was at or near an all-time high; (2) trade was at or near an all-time high; (3) employment was at or near an all-time high; (4) Canadian industry was at its peak; (5) agricultural production was very great and the

Of course, there were anxieties about the future; but to say that there was an emergency at the date of the order in council such as that described by Lord Haldane, and such as to justify an invasion of the provincial legislative field, seems to me to be without foundation and entirely unjustified.

Mr. Speaker, when we rose at six o'clock I had been quoting from the words of a judgment dealing with the emergency transitional powers act and an order in council under that act which have a bearing on the resolution which we are now considering. I propose again to quote from that judgment, and to seek to impress upon hon. members of the house the fact that the words that I now quote do indicate the measure of responsibility which must be assumed by those hon. members who are prepared by their vote to declare that there is an emergency of the kind that would continue these very broad and indefinite powers. I quote from the judgment:
Parliament cannot make an emergency In one sphere an excuse or pretext to invade the provincial legislative field in another sphere. To hold otherwise would be to hold that all parliament required to legally trench upon the provincial field was a colourable excuse; and of course that is contrary not only to common sense, but to the principle underlying the "pith and substance" cases.
What I have read from this judgment indicates the extent to which the emergency which would justify the continuance of emergency powers must, in fact, be a real emergency. When hon. members of the House of Commons vote on a resolution which will have the effect of carrying a stage forward the consideration of a broad omnibus bill of this kind, their vote is not only a vote to deal with the particular subjects contained in the various orders that would be continued under this bill; it is an expression of opinion by hon. members of the House of Commons that this is in fact an emergency that justifies the abandonment for the time being of the division of authority between the dominion and provincial governments, which was laid doum in our constitution.

The judgment which I have quoted does not go so far as to declare that the emergency transitional powers act is ultra vires. The fact that it did not so declare in no way alters the effect of each of the quotations which I have placed before hon. members. They were dealing with an order in council which had been passed under this act. That order in council had the effect of taking over the ownership of large quantities of barley in a limited part of Canada, and of providing the procedure by which that barley could be resold. The appeal court of the province of Manitoba held that the order in council was ultra vires of the government of Canada. They did so on the ground that there was no emergency of the kind that would make necessary steps of that kind. The judges of the appeal court made it clear that they were not dealing with the question whether the emergency transitional powers act is intra vires or ultra vires of the parliament of Canada. They did indicate that there is a very clearly established legal proposition that the courts will not decide against a decision of parliament except on very strong grounds; but in this case the judges made it clear that they were dealing only with the order in council, and they expressed no opinion about the question whether or not the act itself was intra vires.
I mention that pow because I would hope that no hon. member would suggest that the fact that this judgment did not deal with the emergency transitional powers act itself, and the question whether or not it was intra vires of the powers of the Canadian parliament, have nothing to do with the responsibilities of all hon. members to assure themselves that there is in fact an emergency before they continue these wide and dictatorial powers.
The fact is that the judgment went so far as to point out that there was no crisis of the kind that would be required to declare an economic or other emergency of the kind; and since this bill is an omnibus bill dealing with many emergency powers, it would only be in the case of a general economic emergency, or a general emergency of some kind, that hon. members would have the right now to declare as a fact that there is a general emergency which would support the many provisions of these emergency powers.
I hope that no one will suggest that any hon. member who opposes the continuance of these wartime powers is opposing rent control or any other provision to meet the situation which has arisen very largely as a result of the activities of the government itself.

That Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole on the following proposed resolution:

Resolved that it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war.

On that occasion it was made quite clear that the motion of the previous question is a motion to stop the introduction of amendments, but that it permits a general discussion of the whole subject. That argument was also put forward quite competently by the right hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Mackenzie King) as reported on page 4347 of Hansard of 1943. At that time the right hon. member indicated that he clearly accepted the principle that the motion of the previous question is a motion that calls for a general discussion of the main motion but prevents the introduction of amendments. Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should have indicated more clearly the reasons for the remarks I was making. Assume for the sake of argument that this might be a borderline case as to whether or not there is an emergency. There are reasons why this house should be particularly cautious, in the case of this government, in extending powers to them. After all, there must be some borderline cases where there might be difficulty in determining whether there was an emergency that would justify the continuance of the powers, but I submit that there is no such difficulty here. Even if hon. members felt that there was an emergency, I still think it is essential that they should consider what government will be exercising these powers, at least for a short time. That being so, I was addressing my remarks to the conduct of this government in the exercise of powers of this kind and I was indicating the belief in bureaucracy and in centralized control which I think every hon. member should be aware of when he casts his vote on this motion.
It was in that respect that I was indicating the attitude of the Prime Minister in regard

to matters of this kind and his concept of bureaucracy and his concept of his own responsibilities and of the general situation in regard to matters of this nature. When he made the statement to which I have referred, suggesting that if there was any danger of communism in this country it would come because under the Conservative party there would be subservience to the financial interests, I do think that it is important that the members of this house be fully aware of the background of the man who made such a statement and that they should not be in any doubt as to who that man is.
