maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), and his citation, have reminded me of young Lochin-var, and the lines I learned in school:
Oh, young Lochinvar is come out of the west, Through all the wide border his steed was the best:
And save his good broadsword he weapons had none ....
He stayed not for brake, and he stopped not for stone,
He swam the Esk river where ford there was none-
Perhaps I will be in order if I refer to another matter which the Minister of Agriculture discussed in this same debate last February 18. I was surprised that, with respect to the handling of rye in this country-and I am referring to the cereal-he admitted rather boastfully the fact that he was the culprit, for the manner in which rye was handled. I believe it was in the fall of 1947 that we had what was termed a legal racket in this country for some months during the autumn. I remember being taken to task at that time because I referred to the fact that funds were being issued for people to go to the United States to buy rye and bring it into Canada, then reship it to foreign countries, where we had made loans with the taxpayers' money. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) himself said in front of the Minister of Finance, right in the house, that when they made those loans they knew they would not be repaid. Those people were making a profit of about a dollar a bushel on that rye which they brought in from the United States, thereby aggravating our dollar shortage. That was a legalized racket.
I put a question on the order paper in December of 1947, and I have all the answers here. One of the largest shipments was to Poland-about 700,000 bushels. The next was 440,000 bushels to Germany. There were fourteen countries to which rye was shipped; and the funds of the foreign exchange control
Transitional Measures Act board were used-the taxpayers' money. The taxpayers of this country will be assessed for that racket of this government by order in council legislation. Reference was made this afternoon to the decision of the appellate court of Manitoba delivered by Mr. Justice J. E. Adamson. I am sure that that case had to do with orders in council, and he points out how illegal these matters are in this country.
Mr. Watson Sellar, the auditor general, who is above this government, who reports only to parliament, has drawn attention to certain irregularities by order in council in connection with the expenditure of public money.
I do not think I should take further time, as Your Honour has not been very clear in telling me whether I am in order in discussing the United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement. I certainly shall be able to do that on the estimates and prove to the Minister of Trade and Commerce how much that is going to cost the wheat producers of this country. In those three years of 1946, 1947 and 1948 crops it will cost them $721 million, the difference between the figures his parliamentary assistant put on the record and the price of $1.75 per bushel, basis Fort William.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first I should like to know whether I am in order in saying something about the housing situation in Davenport riding. I do not want to go on if I am not, because there is no use being interrupted as the previous speaker has been.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I would say to the hon. member what I have said to other hon. members. I believe it would be much better for him and for everyone if he would wait until the bill is before us so that he will know exactly what controls or orders in council the government wants to continue.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
What I have to say has to do with housing controls. I am one of those hon. members who make exhaustive inquiry into matters I am going to speak about.
I want to digress for a moment and refer to what was said this afternoon by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) about the proposed bridge across the strait of Canso. For fifteen years I fought against the proposal to construct either a causeway or a tunnel and I was pleased to hear the minister announce that the bridge for which I have been fighting for that length of time is now going to be built.
I followed the same plan in connection with housing in Davenport riding. I visited many people and found them up against an appalling housing situation. I am glad the minister of reconstruction is in his seat, although

Transitional Measures Act at the same time I am sorry that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) is not in his seat at the moment. I expected a great deal of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in connection with housing when he was Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. The Minister of Trade and Commerce should have been able to solve the housing problem if any one could. He was a builder and contractor and as far as I can understand he knew all about building. However, he did not do it. I am not going to say whether the present minister of reconstruction can do the job or not. In any event the problem is not being solved.
First, I want to say a word or two as to what the job is. I fear the minister is not conversant with the vast difference between the housing problem faced by a great city like Toronto and the housing problem faced by any one of a thousand smaller places. The problem is different and different methods are required to obtain relief. He may be able to do it. I hope he is.
I called upon one home where a father, mother and seven of a family, a total of nine people, were living in one room, near where I live. Language cannot describe the conditions that exist in a household like that. Language cannot describe what a father and mother are up against under such conditions. I am not going to blame the minister, I am not going to say who is responsible, but that is the situation. That is only one case in many that I know of and perhaps there are thousands throughout Canada.
I called on another family and found eleven living in three small rooms of a humble workingman's home. The first room was entered off the verandah; the second room immediately behind was a living room, dining room and kitchen, and then there was one bedroom. Ordinary language cannot describe just what parents go through under those conditions. Nine boys and girls had to sleep on the floor or wherever they could find room. I am not going to blame anybody for that, but that is the situation. There are hundreds of cases just like that.
I went to visit many families, and I found one home in which there were nine people in two rooms. These are not spectacular cases; they are quite common. The city has become overwhelmingly congested with people coming in from everywhere and trying to get shelter of any kind. That is the problem. What is the minister going to do about it?
I shall make a suggestion in a few minutes as to what might be done. These are just some cases in the multitude of those that exist.
Here is an example not far from where I [Mr. MacNicol.J
live. A man and wife had lived in a house for 27 years. They have a crippled son who is not able to walk or stand up, and a daughter. There were four rooms in the house. The house was sold over their heads and they could not begin to make a down payment on another house because he was a humble moulder in a company with which I am well acquainted. He never made salary enough to permit him to save money to make a down payment.
The purchaser having purchased the house quite legally waited the legal length of time, which I have just forgotten, and then went before a judge who ordered this family, who had lived in the house all those years, to share the space with the buyer. What does that mean? I saw this myself and I know. It would break anyone's heart to see what those people have to go through. The father and mother, the daughter and the son now live in two rooms on the ground floor while the buyer lives upstairs in the two rooms there. The bathroom is upstairs and is used by both families but in order to go upstairs you must pass through the living-dining room of the family downstairs.
The lady of the house has been to see me many times. She is a humble little woman and her heart is broken because they cannot get accommodation anywhere. They simply cannot afford to pay $1,000 down on a house. These are just examples of the multitude of cases that exist. Many men have worked in plants for most of their lives but have never made enough money in order to save sufficient to pay $1,000 or $1,500 down on a house. That case is a sample of many more.
I know of another case of a young soldier who came back with a good record. He brought a bride back with him from the old country. When he came home his people were glad to see him. He brought a bride with him, however, and the bride had to sleep somewhere. When they arrived home the father and mother took in the bride and the son. There were four rooms in the house. There were the father and mother and four children besides the young soldier and his bride, making eight in all. Things went along for a short time, but human flesh and blood cannot endure those conditions and still have peace and happiness, and it was not long until a family row started with the result that the young man and his bride had to get out. They could not get in anywhere. With not less than 15,000 people in the city wanting to move into other places, there was no place for them. The result was that in the end the young woman, and likely a very fine young woman, became heartbroken, and she left Canada and went back to England. That has an effect on family life.

The Rev. Dr. Mutchmor, who I believe is head of the public relations division of the United church, has stated that such cases as that are multitudinous, and that in not less than twenty-five per cent of such homes family life is being broken down.

I would think that whatever the hon. member for Broadview says is correct. I have a very high opinion of what he says, and if he says it is correct then it is correct. Coming back to where I left off, may I say that I would rather help the minister than say anything to hurt his feelings. It does not get us anywhere to do that; it does not help to solve a difficult situation. The examples I have given are illustrations of the situation in a multitude of other cases. What can we do? The hon. member for Broadview interrupted me. Let me refer to what he did when he was mayor of Toronto, and may I say that Toronto never had a better mayor. He was seven times mayor of Toronto, and he was successful because of what he did for the people. He was mayor from 1915 to 1921, and he had all these conditions to contend with. In Toronto they took over land in the city and around the city and installed water, light and gas facilities. They overcame a lot of trouble in that way. There are no more lots, however, in Toronto. I do not know of a lot you can buy at a reasonable price in Toronto today. In the days of Mayor T. L. Church you could buy a fine lot for from $6 to $8 a foot in the part of the city where I live now. That section was opened up by the putting in of sewers, water mains, gas mains, electric light wires and transportation. To a very large extent because of the cheap lots and the services that were provided, the housing problem then was not one-two-three with what it is today.
How can the minister overcome the difficulty? You cannot buy any lots in Toronto. The city bought a block of lots last year and put up a building where the rents are so high that no workingman could rent a place. A workingman should never be asked to pay over $30 or $35, and at the maximum $40 a
Transitional Measures Act month for rent. He cannot make enough to do so. What can the minister do? He could follow the plan that was followed in the days of Mayor T. L. Church. The land around the city of Toronto is built up, but I believe you could go out still further. I understand from the department that last year, through then-boards and other assistance, and through the builders, 80,000 homes were built in Canada.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Eighty-one thousand.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The minimum required today is not less than 250,000, and nearer 500,000 homes. I made a survey in my own riding, which is a workingman's riding. They are wonderful people, carpenters, painters, machinists, moulders, artisans of every description, well-read people. Maybe that is why they always give me such a large majority, and I expect they will do so again. I made a survey of many homes, and what I found- and the minister will find the same thing- is that at the present time the number of people occupying a polling subdivision is approximately 25 per cent more than occupied the same polling subdivision before this crisis arose. That means that, if a subdivision had 500 people living in it, another 125 are crowded in there, or 25 per cent more. That is a staggering difficulty to overcome. These people will all want homes; they will all want to move out and have a home by themselves. All these people living three, four, five and six to a room will want to move out. They should have homes, because the home is the basis of the nation.
I want to suggest to the minister that in the vicinity of Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton -not so much Hamilton-Windsor, where they are fairly congested, Winnipeg and Vancouver, a survey be made to ascertain if it is possible for the department to secure control over large blocks of land in various areas outside the cities. What I have in mind are 200 and 300 acre lots not too far out from the city, but even if they are some distance away that probably can be overcome. I think the minister should then ascertain what it will cost to run water out to those areas, and put in sewers, electricity, gas, schools and so on. I am satisfied that, if that can be done, the average workingman would probably be able to buy a lot for $10 per foot. At the time when the member for Broadview (Mr. Church) was mayor of Toronto the workingman was able to buy a lot for $6 a foot in the vicinity of St. Clair avenue in Toronto. Then these people would have the same opportunity that the people living in my section of the city had when I first went up there. Land was cheap then, and it was the time when many immigrants were coming from the old country. Thousands

Transitional Measures Act and thousands of them were brought in by the former Laurier administration, and they did great things for this country. They bought the lands cheaply and were able to get materials such as lumber, and so on. I have seen them times without number carrying scantling and other pieces of lumber and building material on their shoulders up Dufferin street hill near where I live. I have seen them with parts of plumbing fixtures and other things, and in due course they built homes to live in. It was called shack town, but it was a great credit to the men who came from the old country. They bought the land and built their homes, and today they are all living in nice homes and surroundings. Perhaps we can do the same thing. In any event the situation is nothing short of appalling, and from his close contact with it I am sure the minister must agree with me.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
If the
hon. member would permit a question, I should like to ask whether he has given any consideration to the possibility of anything useful being done in the way of prefabricated houses.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I have. Perhaps I had better continue with what I was saying and come back to that, because prefabrication has been a great study of mine. I would ask the minister to discuss with his officials the possibility of doing something along the line I have suggested. Then I am sure he is aware of what has been done at Three Rivers. I have forgotten the name of the parish priest or the reverend gentleman who organized the opening up of a large area near that city, with homes for workingmen. If they can do it near Three Rivers we should be able to do it near Toronto.
I would particularly suggest that the minister inquire into the matter of services. In Toronto we have no suburban railways. Montreal has, I am glad to say. I am happy that the people of Montreal have insisted on having suburban railways. We have none, so we have no way of running trains out a mile or two or three or four or five. There could be; the northern track would do very well for a suburban railway into York county, where various areas could be built up, each with thousands of houses. I suggest that to the minister in all earnestness. The problem must be solved. It is nothing short of murderous as it is today. My constituency has seventy thousand people in an area four and a half miles long and less than three-quarters of a mile wide, so hon. members will realize how congested it must be. I am thoroughly conversant with conditions there, and I repeat that too frequently they are nothing short of shocking.

My hon. friend asked about prefabricated houses. I do not know why the former Minister of Reconstruction and Supply did not do something in regard to prefabrication, because he was well posted on that subject; he has heard me talking on it before. I saw prefabricated houses on the docks at Quebec, and they were fine little houses too; but we shipped them to France. The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but I believe the price was about $1,500 per house.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes, about that.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Well, why can we not have them in Canada? The timber is all here, the stone is all here, the cement is all here. If we can supply houses for France at $1,500 each, why can we not supply prefabricated houses for the working people of Toronto at $1,500 each? I know all about workingmen. I have been with them all my lifetime, served with them all the way from the bottom to the top. I do not have to take off my hat to anyone when talking about labour, I care not where they come from or where they have been, because with hands and head I have worked with labour. They cannot pay the prices they are being asked today. I do not believe any workingman living can pay seven, eight or nine thousand dollars for a home. So why cannot the government, realizing the situation, come forward with some solution? I do not know how they would go about it, but perhaps it would be by means of a big bonus. I would go for that, or for anything to save the health and lives of our people. I know that for want of homes people of my community are breaking down into old men and women long before their time.
Coming back to the question of prefabrication, I have referred to one type of prefabricated house. The former minister will also remember the big plant just east of Montreal, the name of which I have forgotten.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Fairchild.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes. I went there and discussed the matter with the manager, who showed me several prefabricated aluminum houses, which I think were being sold for around $2,000 to $2,500.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No; about $3,300.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Even that is far short of seven, eight or nine thousand dollars. We have a young minister now, and I would like to see him make a success of it. He has a very good record, and I would rather help him than do anything else. I suggest that he inquire into the matter of prefabricated houses. You may be able to interest some builder of prefabricated houses. I believe a very good prefabricated house is made in London; but I would not go for the fancy

prices they are asking today. Offer an order for five thousand prefabricated houses; perhaps you will get them at the right price. You have to plan not for five thousand but for five hundred thousand homes. The problem is here. It is not going to run away; it is going to get worse every day. Does that answer my hon. friend's question?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes, thank you.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Now I want to say a word about our own mayor of Toronto, who has done a very good job and wants to help all he can. I am sure if the minister made contact with him he would find that Mayor Hiram McCallum would be happy to help in any way possible. He is in despair today because he is right up against it. I used to go home every week end, but now I can only stand to go home every three weeks. When I get home there is too much pressure of all sorts, especially in connection with housing. I am too soft-hearted; I cannot stand the tears of the women when they ask me to help them out. What does Mayor McCallum say?
I quote from the Toronto Telegram?
Unless the federal government primarily, and the provincial government secondarily, provide special and specific co-operation for the Toronto area, Mayor Hiram McCallum despairs of solving the housing problem.
He despairs because he does not know what to do about it. Then again:
The fundamental weakness of the government's program, the mayor told the Telegram today, lies in their attempt to apply the same formula to huge urban areas such as Toronto, as in smaller communities.
Why could not the minister come out boldly with some great plan? The public would support him. That is what they want; someone with vision who will come out and say "This is what I am going to do." There would be no trouble getting the money. It might cost $100,000,000, but that much spent in saving the health and lives of the people of Canada would be well spent. I for one would do all I could to help the minister. All around Toronto they are clamouring for houses. We read the other day that the Lake Shore road is clamouring for 2,000 houses. East Toronto is clamouring for 1,500 houses. York township is clamouring for 2,000 houses.
A short time ago I attended a meeting of the Earlscourt legion, one of the largest in Toronto. About five hundred people were there on two floors, both packed. They had been called to discuss the question of housing, and they had invited Major Harvey Lynes, Colonel Finney and Frank Dearlove. Every now and then this government grants
Transitional Measures Act decorations. If I were in the minister's position I would give decorations to all these men. They deserve them for what they have done to alleviate the appalling suffering of many people in that city. I do not know where any government could get a man with the same sympathy and courtesy and who would make such a genuine effort to try to solve problems as Frank Dearlove has displayed during the last few years. How he lives I do not know, because what he goes through is appalling.
A short time ago there came to my notice the case of a young Scotsman who had been in Canada two years with his wife and two children. There were six people in the house and this young man occupied the upstairs. Some person bought the house. I do not know what the regulations are in this connection, and 1 am not going to find fault with controls, the lack of controls, or advocate more or less controls. The problem is too gigantic to be handled in that manner. Every case has to be considered on its own merits. We may have too much control, but I would fear what might happen if we wiped out all control on housing.
As I said, the house was sold over this young man's head. The tenant downstairs was put out. I used my best judgment and kept the man upstairs from being thrown out. I will say that Mr. Dearlove was able to hold off the sheriff until he could place the man at Long Branch, his wife in a room a few blocks from where she had been living, and the two children with some friends. Consider what that meant to that family. Think of the heartburning pain of the mother and father grieving for the children. The problem is big and it can only be solved by big and fearless methods. Let the minister come forward with something big and fearless and I am sure he will receive the support of the house.
When I commenced my speech I said that I depended on my right hon. friend solving that problem, but he did not do it. He could have done it and I wish he had done it. If he had, it would be a lot easier for the present minister. I have stated the situation and there is no necessity for repeating it. I have mentioned the breaking up of homes and the breaking down of health and family life. I have mentioned the heartburnings of the parents all over the city, not only in Davenport riding. I believe 15,000 people have to find homes in the city of Toronto by May first.
Coming back to what I said a few moments ago, I suggest to the minister that he face up to the problem in a big way, much the same as was done years ago. It has been done at
14G4	HOUSE OF
Transitional Measures Act Three Rivers and elsewhere. In connection with housing projects, the government should try to obtain large blocks of land near a big city. Land is unobtainable in the city and no one could pay the price asked for land in Toronto today. A working man can pay $6, $8 or $10 per foot and he can pay up to $2,500 for a home. He might even be able to go as high as $3,000. If you wanted to make it a prefabricated scheme, prefabrication ought to be considered and the plan of the government should be not to build 80,000 homes in 1949, but to build at least 150,000, because we are going to need up to 500,000 before long. I think I have done the best I can, in a pleasant way and in a helpful manner, to present the problem and suggest a remedy.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a short contribution to this debate, possibly more out of habit than for any other reason. I have spoken on this subject since the beginning of this parliament. I have rebelled against the attitude of the government, without much success, and have sought, by such slender means as are within my power, to bring it to a better sentiment.
I was mildly interested a short time ago in turning to the debates of the early autumn of 1945 when this parliament was newly elected and when these post-war emergencies were first thought of as a counter-agent to political crises. I found that I had expressed myself with what seems to have been considered as undue vigour because the right hon. Minister of Agriculture said in reply that he thought a good deal of heat had been generated in considering a measure that was to last but a few months. He made some casual and passing remarks about the spirit of Liberalism which animated his party and which precluded it from pursuing at any length a course of action which would impose controls upon the country.
The right hon. minister said: This bill definitely says what we are doing. It is just what the preamble outlines, namely, asking the house to permit the government to continue in existence the orders in council which were passed during the war and which it is necessary to have continued for a few months after the war. The phrase "a few months" was reiterated a number of times during the minister's remarks, as he went on to recount the achievements of the government. It was pointed out how much more successful the war which had recently come to an end had been waged than the first war and how much more complete had been the discipline in national affairs as a result of the imposition of controls. Some figures were mentioned as [Mr. MacNicol.l

to prices. Since then, of course, prices have soared to such heights that the prices which followed the first war seem almost valleys in the presence of the mountains of the second war.
Be that as it may, here we are four years after the war and we are asked once more to bow our necks to the yoke of controls. I for one cannot do it gladly. I think a reading of history shows us that the general record of mankind has been one of great poverty and that by far the most fruitful method ever developed to make the world richer has been that of leaving men free, within the limits of the civil and criminal law, to engage their energies on their own account and for their own reward. This discovery was made against the instinct of kings and other rulers who, like the rulers of today, found it very difficult, found it very much against the grain, to leave any part of trade or manufacturing free from their interference.
Something was said earlier in the day about the case which was recently decided by the appeal court in Manitoba. I think it should be of some interest to the house, and I think it may serve as a warning to future generations, if we examine briefly this great record, because it shows the development of a state of mind which throws into relief how contagious and how inflammatory is the inclination to dominate and control once it has become the practice of a government or of a party.
Your Honour will recall that legislation was passed which made it incumbent upon the growers of certain grains to sell them to the government. There was a man by the name of Nolan, a rather good name-who unfortunately lived in Chicago-I say unfortunately because I wish that he who had the spirit and the courage to stand up against the government for the first time, and hale it before the courts of the land, had been a Canadian. This is rather a sad sidelight. It shows how soon people become accustomed to this kind of thing, how soon their fibre, if not broken, is weakened, and how independent people soon become accustomed to being jerked around on a cord. In any event, this gentleman by the name of Nolan was a grain merchant; he held some 40,000 bushels of barley at Fort William, which he wished eventually to ship to the United States. On March 17, 1947-and that is another good day-the wheat board demanded that all commercial holders of barley should sell their coarse grains to it, at a fixed price, and barley at sixty-four and three-quarter cents a bushel, and at the same time established prices for the sale of that same com-

modity anywhere from ninety cents to ninety-three cents per bushel, the spread going into the coffers of this government agency.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No, it did not.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Of all the holders of barley Nolan was the only one who refused to comply.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The spread went back to the farmers.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The spread went back to the farmers after the government, and the agency which represented it, had chipped off its share of expenses and the incidentals which go with it, and at a time when the government determined it was good to send it back, and it generally is not good to send it back until the eve of an election.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: And the barley went down to feed the livestock in your district.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The livestock in my district has been so scantily fed that that portion of it which was not starved to death, because the farmers could not buy feed for the price the government allowed them for their butter, had to be sold across the international border. This has left the farmers of my district in a very sad plight, which I think they will remember for some time.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Nevertheless that is what fed them.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
But to continue with Mr. Nolan and what happened on March 17; to make it brief, he contended that there was no emergency and that in consequence the legislation which had been enacted was without binding effect, and that therefore his barley was his to deal with, to trade in and to deliver to whom he saw fit, as up until a few years ago every Canadian thought was his inherent right. He went before the courts; and after making the investigation which was placed on the record this afternoon, the courts came to the conclusion that Nolan was right, that there was not any emergency, that Nolan owned his barley to do with it as he pleased.
At the moment I am not speaking of the finding of the court. The point that I wish to bring before the house is the argument which was advanced by the government; it shows a frame of mind, it shows a domineering attitude that is, in my submission, totally unbecoming to the administrators of a free country.
To defend the Nolan case the government retained the counsel for the wheat board. He represented the federal government, in the case and, as the record shows, he put forward this argument. At the outset he said that the court, in considering the validity of the transi-
Transitional Measures Act tional act, might hear evidence on the question whether there was or was not a national emergency which would justify the passing of the act; and second, that the court might also hear evidence on the question whether, if there had been such an emergency, it had ceased to exist, or whether it was still in existence; and thirdly, he agreed also that the court, notwithstanding the declaration in the preamble to the act, might hold that there was an emergency, or decide that there was no emergency, or that it had ceased to exist if the evidence warranted such a finding. This seemed fair enough, but it was what followed that was most astounding. When he came to the order in council, 1292, he advanced this startling argument. He said:
If the act is within the powers of parliament because there is a national emergency, no matter what that emergency may be. the court might not inquire if the order in council were valid.
That, if one really seizes the significance of it, is, it seems to me, the acme of arrogance. The argument, if valid, would deny the courts the exercise of that judicial power and discretion which are the very point and purpose of the existence of the courts. It would mean that once there was an emergency, for any reason whatever-an epidemic of measles, a flood or a fire-the government would be entirely free to pass orders in council, no matter what their bearing upon or relation to the particular emergency. He urged that it is "not pertinent to the judiciary to consider the wisdom or the propriety of the particular policy which is embodied in the emergency legislation." (
I cite this because it appears in the brief; and it seemed to me to set forth so perfectly the frame of mind which the government has developed. It is impossible for anyone longer to reason with it or to deal with it on a man-to-man basis.
We are confronted again with the fundamental question of freedom. Again we are asked to yield up that freedom which has been ours for an indeterminate period. We are asked to permit others to manage our affairs for us, without any opportunity of restraint or control from us-the people of Canada, and their elected representatives. What we need today in Canada is not more controls, but a government with nerve enough to banish and to abolish controls. We have staggered along for several years under controls; but I for one do not yet know where those controls have succeeded anywhere.
They have broken down in foreign trade. My delightful friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has to make speeches in the house several times a week to pacify
1466	HOUSE OF
Transitional Measures Act the people whom he thought he was benefiting by his controls and who are now out of money and highly disgruntled and dissatisfied with him. We have rental controls; we have building controls; and there is a shortage of housing. There is a dearth of building. We have financial controls and we are short of dollars. I would be most interested to know wherein this whole practice of controls has yielded that meed of relief and good government which I am willing to think those who indulged in these expedients hoped would be derived from them.
The malady is contagious and self-propagating. Having been put into a supreme position the government have taxed and taxed, and found some reason for seeking to manage other people's affairs, on an assumption, which seems to me an illusion, that they have qualities which enable them more successfully to administer other people's affairs than the people whose affairs they are administering.
I am going to suggest that the government reverse its policy. It has tried about everything so far-everything but letting the people manage their own affairs. I suggest that we go back for a short time to those good days when honest and competent people were permitted to look after their own business, and that this paternal government seek other pastimes, and other fields of amusement than attempting to manage the private affairs of the discontented people of Canada.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to compliment the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) upon the masterful way he presented to the house views which I am sure will claim the attention and be the concern of every hon. member.
Emergency control measures in themselves lend a sense of anxiety to those who are delegating to the administration this overall authority to coritrol the welfare of the nation.
I believe most hon. members would agree that some measure of control may be necessary as a result of the present administration's policies, inasmuch as they have sought to control the economic life of the nation, which procedure has resulted in placing Canada in an economic strait-jacket today. As a matter of fact because of the nature of the controls, and the over-all authority delegated to the administration, it is practically impossible for business to plan, with any degree of confidence, for a long period of time. Yet those who have been responsible for the development and progress of this nation have been men who had vision and who were able to plan with some sense of confidence that their plans would not arbitrarily be interfered with.


Yet we find in this measure-the daddy of them all-which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) now seeks to introduce by way of resolution, machinery whereby the government can do almost anything a dictatorial government could do. I suggest the nature of the control measures, which have played such a dominant part in the life of this nation has affected the over-all picture, has been responsible for the labour unrest, for the high cost of living and for all the other ills which are properly charged to the present administration.
This type of control robs people of their incentive, their ambition, and their desire to do those things which would make Canada robust and strong. I can think back to those tragic days of the war when measures of control for national security and safety were necessary. At that time we were concerned with one common objective, and we were able to obtain the help and the advice of the most outstanding men in Canada. It was that measure of co-operation and that desire to make a full-out contribution to a common cause which first placed us in the position in which we find ourselves today.
We have moved a considerable distance from those days, and yet we can picture the psychological effect, not only upon the people whose lives are restricted by these controls but upon the administration itself. They have arrived at the place where they are fearful of entrusting to the citizens of Canada the right to plan and think for themselves with some degree of certainty, the right to govern themselves within the law.
These control measures have added to the cost of government and they have contributed in no way to its efficiency. They have caused the machinery of government to become cluttered up with bureaucrats, and as someone has said, I think quite properly, with those people who go around snooping into other people's business. The time has arrived when an honest man feels that he must adopt some method to avoid being called to task by these government bureaucrats.
As I have already intimated, the effect of taxation has been to increase the cost of living because it has restricted production. It has created a degree of scarcity in a land of plenty. How imbued the government have become with their present authority and their indispensability is evidenced by the statements which have been made by ministers of the crown, particularly the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), who has intimated on more than one occasion that they felt it necessary to drain off, from the individual, purchasing power which was rightly his in order that they might seek to legislate still further and

increase the cost of living, which incidentally has had its effect on the volume of production.
We find that one control leads to another. Until this government finds some means of restoring to the people of Canada that sense of freedom which in days gone by we have admired as being one of the great features of democracy, until this government finds some means of restoring the sense of justice which the people expect under a democracy, there will simply be a nullification of their ambitions and desires.
Our concern is to legislate for the people of Canada so that they may not be unnecessarily restricted but rather encouraged to go forward. Foreign capital should be encouraged to invest in Canada, risk capital as it were, so that we may develop our great natural resources. It has been proved conclusively that while capital is willing to risk itself in ventures that may not bear rich fruits, no capital is prepared to risk itself with a government that interferes with individual rights and personal freedom.
Having regard to the statement made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), and recognizing as I do that there may be necessity to continue some controls, I submit that it is unfair to members of this House of Commons to bring in a blanket bill. Each control should be presented separately so that it could be debated on its merits and dealt with individually. I sometimes wonder if we are fully conscious of the measure of authority we are placing in the hands of the government of Canada.
I would recall to hon. members that in England today bills are before the House of Commons to nationalize certain industries. It would seem that the government of Canada was seeking to circumvent parliament and delegate to itself authority so broad that, once possessed, they would enjoy the right to nationalize any industry which might suit their purpose. We have plenty of evidence that in the past these powers have been used too arbitrarily, and I fear that they might again be used in that way.
It places in the hands of the administration the type of monopolistic control which I noticed, in reviewing the contribution made by the leader of the C.C.F. socialist party, he hopes will be continued and extended. I say that if there is any one monopoly we have reason to fear, it is government monopoly. Where this type of nationalization has taken place, those who were loud in support are beginning to fear its lack of efficiency and bureaucratic control.
Workers in the old country who clamoured for the nationalization of the coal mines now realize that they are unable to find fault
Transitional Measures Act with the owners because the government owns the coal mines. They are unable to approach anyone nearby to seek better working conditions, because any member of the union who has accepted an official position is no longer a member. The only way they can get satisfaction is to carry their complaint to London, which means sending a deputation under considerable difficulty.
I realize that there are some types of public ownership, especially those having to do with water power and other items of what might be considered a public utility character, which might recommend themselves to hon. members, but even in that regard I think we should go slow and give the matter careful consideration. I submit that the resolution which contemplates the introduction of a bill should be viewed in the light of the representations made by hon. members of the Progressive Conservative party, particularly the leader of the opposition. I would urge the government to accept his advice and break down the resolution into a number of bills so that each matter may be dealt with on its merits. That in turn will provide citizens by law with the right of appeal so that they may enjoy the protection and consideration of the courts of the land. It seems to me that we have arrived at a point where the government is still suffering from a war complex. Controls of a nature acceptable during the war are being continued. Yet we can understand the part controls have played in the very difficult situation we find ourselves in at the present time. Therefore we find the government reluctant to release, from their over-all authority, the measure of control they have been able to exercise over the economic life of the nation, and indeed over the very lives of individual citizens.
Measures of this character, while considered to be for the common good in the first instance, establish a precedent and place the affairs of the nation in grave jeopardy. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, while we may have a great deal of confidence in one another as private citizens, delegated authority of the character which is sought through this resolution, to be followed by a bill, simply makes the administration more conscious of that exercise of authority and restraint which they have practised with abandon, and without regard to the best interests of the nation. It has in the main served selfish interests to a greater extent than it has served the great masses of the Canadian people.
I agree with the hon. member for Stan-stead (Mr. Hackett) that sooner or later the administration will have to demonstrate a
1468	HOUSE OF
Transitional Measures Act degree of courage, and will have to be prepared to relieve the country of all restrictions and give competitive enterprise an opportunity to work on its own behalf, so that it may be capable of competing in highly competitive markets, not only in Canada but in other parts of the world. One of the things we have suffered from most, in my opinion, and in the opinion of many substantial economists in Canada, is the fact that, through authority of this character, the government is able to interfere with the normal level of our currency and exchange. That has indeed robbed our producers, industrialists and businessmen of the opportunity to seek new markets in distant parts of the world, inasmuch as, while the United States dollar was accepted as the standard of value, we had enjoyed a distinct advantage on a competitive basis in all markets of the world, and the productive capacity of the nation had become very great indeed.
We are rich in natural resources, so much so that it is a challenge to the young men and women of this great nation, and a challenge to those who are now seeking to make their homes and earn their livelihood in Canada. This great country offers them an opportunity, but if we rob them of their incentive, if we rob them of their vision, if we rob them of their ambition to toil, in other words, if through centralized authority we encourage them to become leaners rather than leaders, the nation will suffer and we will be the losers in the long run. In the main, man is prepared to accept the challenge of existence as he seeks to improve his own position in the ordinary course of his everyday activities. But if you set up laws delegating to some central authority the right to control your very existence, then it is difficult to plan or to provide the funds and capital that it costs to establish yourself in any particular line of business.
I do not intend to detain the house longer than to urge again that the government break these bills down instead of bringing in what has been referred to as an omnibus bill, a broad over-all authority, all-inclusive of certain control measures which in our own good judgment may have some merit, but also including others which have little or no appeal, and others which should not be there at all. It is unfair to the members of the House of Commons to suggest that, because we are opposed to this bill, we are opposed to rent control. I think we all realize that a very chaotic condition would result if rent control were removed immediately. Yet it is the control of rents and the over-all authority over dwellings generally which has played a great part in creating the absolute confusion which exists in housing today. I 

think a survey would reveal that there are probably more people living as single occupants of dwellings today than for many long years, if not in the history of Canada. The reason for that is that, while a person may have a flat or room and be willing to share accommodation and take people in, such people may prove to be unsuitable, and under the type of controls which we have now it is impossible to get them out. Therefore people are fearful of offering to share their dwellings with others.
I mention that merely to try to indicate that controls in themselves are bad. A regulated control by means of a statute which sets in motion a process of law to deal with these various measures would probably have some appeal. At any rate, if these bills were separated, we would not have to deal with them collectively, but would have an opportunity to deal with each individual item on its own merits. Through this measure our socialist friends feel that we have to a large extent eliminated competition. Competition after all is a regulative force. It fixes the value of things, and without that regulative force you have no standard by which to fix the value of anything. From my own experience I have learned that the more you interfere with natural laws the more difficult it becomes to govern. There is a knack in doing things, the knack of knowing how; but the present administration, with the experience born of years of regulation and control, are reluctant to restore to the Canadian people that measure of freedom our gallant sons and daughters fought to preserve in this country.
Surely the time has come when we must trust our fellow Canadians. Surely we should be able to say that business can be entrusted with the management of its own affairs. The sooner that measure of responsibility is restored to business the sooner we will break what I consider to be the deadlock we are in at the present time, with a regulating state, socialistic in its outlook and indeed restrictive in its results. I simply ask that this House of Commons have restored to it that measure of responsibility which every member came here prepared to assume, and for which he is prepared to answer to his constituents.
How can the government present a measure in omnibus form when, as I have intimated already, it may contain some measures which should be continued and at the same time other objectionable measures which we feel are bad for the general welfare of the nation? It is impossible for us to separate them. We must deal with them collectively and accept them all. It is a take it or leave it proposition which does not appeal t6 me nor, I am sure, to any other

responsible member who wishes to have some knowledge of the extent to which the government proposes to proceed. If they would deal with these matters in statutory form, presenting each measure separately so it may be dealt with on its merits, I feel we could make greater progress. The government would feel more secure because they had restored to Canada some semblance of responsible government, and to the members of this house the opportunity to share in that responsibility.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, upon this resolution the government hopes to found a bill which will give it authority to continue, during the fifth year of peace, a residuum of five unnatural wartime controls. As the house knows from the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) the other day, these are controls over steel, over the prices of certain commodities, over timber, over priorities and over residential rents.
I think it is obvious to all hon. members now, though until this year it was only obvious to those in this party, that the Canadian people do not want controls. Rather they want ample supplies of those things now apparently in short supply, so that in the opinion of the government, there is a necessity for a continuation of these unnatural controls. Therefore there are two sides to this control measure. The first is: Are the conditions such that a continuation of controls is necessary, and arising out of that, what conditions cause these shortages and create this necessity? Secondly, and to my mind of much more importance, is the question: What is this government doing to stimulate the production of those commodities apparently in short supply so we may be certain of getting rid of the controls the Canadian people do not want? It is to that side of the medal, namely the production side, that I want to address my remarks this evening.
I was surprised that in introducing this measure the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) failed to give any indication of what they were going to do in order to be able to abandon these unnatural controls. They simply came into the house, made short statements indicating what controls they wanted to continue, suggested that they wanted to continue them for one year, and then sat down. In my view it would be very wrong for hon. members to be satisfied with statements like those. You see, Mr. Speaker, if we give this government the powers they are asking for; if we simply pass these control measures on the basis that they are appar-
Transitional Measures Act ently necessary; if we do not demand from the ministers at this time an explanation as to what they are going to do to get rid of their control measures; then we will not have another chance to get at them for another year. At this moment the government is in the hands of parliament. The government is coming into this house asking parliament for a favour. When a government needs authority from the house it is much more likely to listen sympathetically to the views of the members of parliament. When they have the power and can exercise it independently of parliament they can remain in their seats smiling and pay no attention to what members of this house bring to their attention.
Therefore if we as private members of this house-and of course I am referring to private members on the government side as well as on this side-neglect this opportunity of impressing upon the government the views of the people, if we let them get away too easily with their continuation of control measures, we will not have the opportunity again for a very long time. We will not be able to force the government to take a positive view of this control problem. We will not be able to force them to adopt the necessary productive policies so that the dead hand of control may be removed from our free economy.
I want to suggest, Mr. Speaker, through you to the members of the house that, before the vote is taken on this resolution, we should hear from the ministers of the government, who are responsible for the production of these articles in respect of which controls are to be continued, how they are going to bring about adequate supplies of these articles so that these unnatural controls can be dropped during the present year. If they do not satisfy us we should not give them the power to continue the control measures, but we should take this opportunity of defeating the government and placing in office a government which will have a positive approach to such problems as steel production and housing. Such a government would see to it that before the year is out there would be no need for controls in Canada.
You see, Mr. Speaker, although this measure is only to be continued for one year, we have been given no indication by the government that it intends to make sure it does not have to come back next year for another helping. As the member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) has pointed out, ever since 1945 we have been told these controls were only necessary for a few months. These measures have been renewed from year to year and we were told that at the end of each year these things

maintopic: X470 HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Every year the government comes before us and asks for this power for one more year. On this side of the house we have voted for the control measures in certain years, relying upon that promise that they were only required for a period of a year. Each time we do that, the government finds it too easy to sit down and do nothing about production. Each time we give the government the authority it must seek from us, we lose our power over it. This year, for my part at least, I will not be satisfied to give them the authority unless they show me that they propose to do something to make sure there will be no necessity for requesting this authority next year.

maintopic: X470 HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: I should like to say to the member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) that I am conceding nothing of the sort. I am asking him, as a private member of parliament and not as a member of the government, and as one who I feel sure does not believe in controls any more than I do, to defeat the government on this resolution so we will be sure they do not come back next year, or even after Easter.

speechtext: Pardon the interruption, but will the member permit a question? As a Vancouver member, I know that any member who opposes rental controls during this session will not be here at the next session.

maintopic: X470 HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: No responsible person in this country, in view of the chaotic state of housing in the country, could oppose rent control at this moment. It is for that reason I am taking part in this debate on the resolution. I do not believe in perpetual rent control. I want to see rent control discontinued at the proper moment. I want to see an adequate supply of housing for the Canadian people so there will be no need for rent control. From what I have seen during the last four years there is no realization on the part of the government that they have a responsibility for the production of houses.
